claims.text: Random atomic mixing in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs creates local lattice distortions.
Random atomic mixing in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs creates orbital hybridizations.
The lattice distortions and orbital hybridizations tune the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates such as acetaldehyde and acetate.
Reducing the Pt fraction relative to the equiatomic alloy will strengthen the binding of oxygenated intermediates.
Stronger binding of oxygenated intermediates will lower catalytic activity.
Stronger binding of oxygenated intermediates will lower catalytic selectivity.
The randomly mixed structure alters the alloy's d-band electronic structure.
Changes in d-band electronic structure modulate the sites and adsorption energies available to ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
In the equiatomic alloy, the multielement cocktail effect balances electron-donating and electron-withdrawing characteristics of the constituent metals.
This electronic balance optimizes the binding energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Reducing Pt content disrupts the electronic synergy present in the equiatomic alloy.
Excessively strong adsorption hinders desorption or further oxidation of oxygenated intermediates.
Hindered desorption or oxidation of intermediates reduces catalytic turnover.
Pt-reduced catalysts will exhibit lower ECSA-normalized ethanol-oxidation current densities than the equiatomic baseline.
Pt-reduced catalysts will exhibit greater accumulation of strongly adsorbed intermediates than the equiatomic baseline.
Reducing the Pt fraction will decrease cycling durability relative to the equiatomic baseline.
The equiatomic PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has an optimal balance of adsorption energies and catalytic activity according to prior tests.
The proposed relationship should hold near ambient temperature and below approximately 1.0 V versus RHE when the disordered solid-solution state is maintained.
Significant phase ordering or phase separation may invalidate the proposed relationship.
Keeping the operating temperature below 80 degrees Celsius avoids thermally induced ordering.
